record.final_answer:
No, that wouldn't work. The plan breaks two limits of Kestrune at the same time.

1. **No network filesystems.** Kestrune 3.2 doesn't support NFS or SMB. The shared mount is `/mnt/shared/ingest`, an NFS export from fs-01 (`config/worker.toml:2`, README).
2. **Only one writer per database.** Kestrune takes an exclusive file lock, so only one process can write to a database. If workers on ingest-a and ingest-b both write to it, one of them will be locked out. And because file locking over NFS is unreliable, the lock might not hold, and both could write and corrupt the data.

What you're proposing is the setup the README describes today. A note from an earlier session already concluded that Kestrune can't back the store as deployed. That note cites the Kestrune limits page (docs.kestrune.example/limits) as of 2026-08-30. I didn't check the docs again today, so if Ops is planning a different Kestrune version, it's worth a quick look.

If you want to keep Kestrune, here are some options:
- **A separate database on local disk for each host.** Each worker writes only to its own Kestrune database on local storage. This works if a batch always goes to the same host, for example by routing on batch ID in the queue. Local disk also makes it easier to meet the "survives power loss" requirement than NFS does.
- **One writer service.** A single process owns the Kestrune database, and both workers send it their writes over RPC. That makes the writer a single point of failure and puts a network round trip into every one of the ~300 writes/s, each up to 6 MiB.
- **A different store.** If both hosts really need to write to shared state, use something built for several network clients, such as Redis, Postgres, or an object store. A storage engine that runs inside the process, like Kestrune, isn't built for that.
